text: A collective communication involves {{c1::all the processes in a communicator}}. Point-to-point calls such as \(\mathrm{MPI\_Send}\) and \(\mathrm{MPI\_Recv}\) involve {{c2::two processes}}.
extra: The study guide asks which ranks call a collective. Every rank in the communicator calls it, rank 0 included.

text: Rank 0 calls \(\mathrm{MPI\_Reduce}\) and rank 1 tries to match it with \(\mathrm{MPI\_Recv}\). This program is erroneous, because every process must call {{c1::the same collective function}}.
extra: Pacheco says a program like this will likely hang or crash.

text: After \(\mathrm{MPI\_Reduce}\), the combined result is stored only on {{c1::the destination process}}. After \(\mathrm{MPI\_Allreduce}\), it is stored on {{c2::every process in the communicator}}.
extra: Use Allreduce when every process needs the total to continue its own computation.

text: \(\mathrm{MPI\_Allreduce}\) takes the same arguments as \(\mathrm{MPI\_Reduce}\) without {{c1::the destination process}}, because every process gets the result.
extra: Lecture 10's example passes &tmpVal, &sum, 1, \(\mathrm{MPI\_DOUBLE}\), \(\mathrm{MPI\_SUM}\) and the communicator, with no rank argument.

text: Lecture 10 calls \(\mathrm{MPI\_Allreduce}\) a {{c1::butterfly}} reduction. In a butterfly, the processes {{c2::exchange}} partial results, so every process ends with the full sum.
extra: The Lecture 10 diagram draws a tree reduce to process 0 and then a reversed tree back out, which Pacheco Fig 3.8 calls a global sum followed by distribution. Pacheco keeps the name butterfly for the exchange pattern in Fig 3.9.

text: The \(\mathrm{data\_p}\) argument of \(\mathrm{MPI\_Bcast}\) is an {{c1::input}} on the source process and an {{c2::output}} on every other process.
extra: The source sends the contents of that buffer, and every other process receives into its own copy of it.

text: In \(\mathrm{Get\_input}\), only rank 0 reads a, b and n with scanf. The \(\mathrm{MPI\_Bcast}\) calls are {{c1::outside}} the \(\mathrm{my\_rank} == 0\) test, so {{c2::every rank}} calls them.
extra: Rank 0 sends as the source, and the other ranks receive. If only rank 0 called \(\mathrm{MPI\_Bcast}\), the other ranks would never get the values.

text: \(\mathrm{MPI\_Bcast}\) sends {{c1::the same data}} to every process. \(\mathrm{MPI\_Scatter}\) sends each process {{c2::a different chunk}} of one array.
extra: Pacheco's example is a 10,000-component vector on 10 processes. Broadcasting it makes every process store all 10,000 components when it only works on 1000.

text: Ranks on machines joined by a slow network must sum \(g(a[i])\) over a large array. The best design has each rank sum {{c1::its own block}}, then {{c2::one \(\mathrm{MPI\_Reduce}\) call}} combines the local sums on rank 0.
extra: This is study guide practice question 1, answer D. Sending every element, or calling \(\mathrm{MPI\_Allreduce}\) after every element, sends one message per element over the slow network.

text: Lecture 11 improves the MPI trapezoid program twice. Rank 0's loop of sends of a, b and n becomes {{c1::\(\mathrm{MPI\_Bcast}\)}}, and the linear receive-and-add loop on rank 0 becomes {{c2::\(\mathrm{MPI\_Reduce}\)}}.
extra: The study guide calls this the typical collective pattern. Broadcast the parameters once, compute locally, then combine with one Reduce or Allreduce.

text: With 8 processes, a linear global sum makes rank 0 do {{c1::7}} receives and adds. A tree-structured sum reduces rank 0's work to {{c2::3}} receives and adds.
extra: In the tree, the pairs in each phase add at the same time, and no other process does more than 2 receives and adds.

text: With a count greater than 1, \(\mathrm{MPI\_Reduce}\) combines arrays {{c1::element by element}}, so one vector per process adds up into one vector on the destination process.
extra: Lecture 10 says a count of 1 sends a single variable from each process, and a larger count sends an array.

text: Collective calls don't use {{c1::tags}}. MPI matches them only by the communicator and {{c2::the order in which each process makes the calls}}.
extra: Point-to-point calls match on communicator, source and tag.

text: Every rank must pass the same {{c1::\(\mathrm{dest\_process}\)}} to \(\mathrm{MPI\_Reduce}\). If rank 0 passes 0 and rank 1 passes 1, the program is erroneous and will likely hang or crash.
extra: Pacheco's rule is that the arguments each process passes to a collective must be compatible.

text: In \(\mathrm{MPI\_Scatter}\), \(\mathrm{send\_count}\) is the number of items sent to {{c1::each process}}, not the size of the whole array. For a block split of n items it is {{c2::\(n/\mathrm{comm\_sz}\)}}.
extra: The first piece goes to process 0, the source included, the next to process 1, and so on. Pacheco notes this simple version needs n to divide evenly by \(\mathrm{comm\_sz}\).

text: In \(\mathrm{MPI\_Gather}\), every process sends its chunk, and only {{c1::the destination process}} ends up with the assembled array. The \(\mathrm{recv\_count}\) argument is the number of items from {{c2::each process}}.
extra: Gather is the reverse of scatter, with the same argument shape. A common use is assembling results on rank 0 for printing.

text: The trapezoidal rule splits \([a, b]\) into n trapezoids of equal base width \(h = {{c1::\frac{b-a}{n} }}\).
extra: Narrower trapezoids give a better approximation, because their over- and under-estimates average out.

text: Each rank integrates \(\mathrm{local\_n} = {{c1::n/\mathrm{comm\_sz} }}\) trapezoids, starting at \(\mathrm{local\_a} = {{c2::a + \mathrm{my\_rank} \cdot \mathrm{local\_n} \cdot h}}\).
extra: It ends at \(\mathrm{local\_b} = \mathrm{local\_a} + \mathrm{local\_n} \cdot h\). The slides assume n divides evenly by \(\mathrm{comm\_sz}\) to keep the code short.
